Day 2, tick 280 (9:30am): The Peach Orchard salient collapses and the III Corps line gives way from the south toward Cemetery Ridge. Graham is wounded and captured. The 141st Pennsylvania, at the angle, loses 150 of the 198 engaged (75.7 percent in Fox's table), the second-highest regimental percentage on the Union side after the 1st Minnesota.

Day 2, tick 240 (6:10am): About 11 a.m. Birney orders Colonel Berdan to feel the enemy beyond the Union left. Berdan takes 100 men of the 1st U.S. Sharpshooters, with the 3rd Maine in support, down the Emmitsburg road. In the woods beyond they run into three Confederate columns changing direction by the right flank, attack them, and after a sharp fight withdraw; Berdan reports to Birney about 2 p.m.

Day 2, tick 301 (7:10pm): Hancock establishes Colonel Willard's brigade on the line the III Corps had left, with no troops on its right or left. The brigade charges and drives back the enemy; Willard is killed by a shot from a Confederate battery, and Colonel Sherrill takes the brigade.

Day 3, tick 546 (11:45am): STANNARD'S VERMONTERS HIT THE FLANK. The 14th Vermont fires from the line; Stannard orders the 13th, which changes front forward on its first company, and the 16th, which does the same on the 13th's left at right angles to the main line, onto the flank of the Confederate column. Hancock reports that the oblique fire of the Vermonters made the troops on that flank double toward their left.

Day 3, tick 505 (8:30am): Heth's division under Pettigrew, in two lines, and part of Pender's division under Trimble (Lane's and Scales's brigades) are posted on Seminary Ridge on Pickett's left; Wilcox's brigade is ordered to move in rear of Pickett's right flank. // No Confederate count of the column appears in the reports read; Hancock estimated the attackers at more than 15,000 (OR 27/1 p.373).

Day 2, tick 315 (12:15pm): Greene's brigade, entrenched on the hill, repels Johnson's attacks, extending its line and strengthened by the detachments sent to it. Steuart's brigade of Johnson's division reaches the works at the foot of the hill that the XII Corps had left.

Day 3, tick 538 (11:05am): PICKETT'S CHARGE BEGINS. About three p.m. the assaulting column steps off Seminary Ridge, in line of battle, toward Cemetery Ridge: Pickett's division in front, Heth's under Pettigrew on its left, part of Pender's under Trimble in support, Wilcox's brigade behind Pickett's right. // Contested: the number (Hancock estimated more than 15,000; Lee and Longstreet give none) and the hour (about 2:00 to 3:00 p.m. in different accounts).

Day 1, tick 27 (7:15am): The Iron Brigade (2nd and 7th Wisconsin, 19th Indiana and 24th Michigan in line; the 6th Wisconsin has been held back as reserve) charges into the woods against Archer's brigade, which has crossed the Willoughby Run. // The Iron Brigade wore the black Hardee hat of the regular army; a Confederate cry that these were not militia is a postwar tradition.

Day 3, tick 522 (9:50am): Many Confederate shells pass over the crest and fall among the horses, caissons and limbers behind the line; Hunt writes that the whole slope behind the crest was swept by shot, and that the fire was 'too much dispersed' to produce the intended effect. // Hunt counts three battery commanders killed in the whole day's artillery fight and a great many horses lost.

Day 3, tick 544 (11:35am): Confederate assault line reaches the Emmitsburg Road and crosses the fencing. Heavy casualties from Union artillery and musketry. Kemper's brigade begins obliquing left toward the Copse of Trees -- exposing its right flank.

Day 1, tick 38 (8:10am): The fighting on the pike dies down. Doubleday reforms the I Corps on McPherson's and Seminary Ridges; Howard arrives about 11:30 a.m. and takes command of the field as senior officer. Heth, whose division had been repulsed, rests his men in line for an hour or more before ordering the next attack with Pender's division in support. // The lull lasted until Ewell's corps appeared on the Union right in the early afternoon.

Day 1, tick 68 (10:40am): As the troops fall back through the streets, a section of Dilger's battery (Battery I, 1st Ohio) is planted on an eminence near the square and helps hold the enemy in check while the baggage wagons and ambulances withdraw.

Day 1, tick 64 (10:20am): Pender's division (Perrin's, Lane's, Thomas's and Scales's brigades) comes up against the I Corps' line on McPherson's and Seminary Ridges. Perrin's South Carolinians carry the ridge near the seminary; Scales is wounded and his North Carolina brigade is hit hard, the Confederate return counting 424 killed and wounded in it.

Day 2, tick 334 (9:15pm): Meade calls the corps commanders to a council at his headquarters. He puts three questions: whether to stay or retire, whether to attack or await attack, and how long to wait. Gibbon, Williams, Birney, Sykes, Newton, Howard, Hancock, Sedgwick and Slocum answer; all favor staying, and most favor waiting to be attacked. // The pencil minutes found among Meade's papers record each reply (OR 27/1 p.73-74); Newton called the position bad and Hancock was puzzled about retiring. The remark that Lee would attack the center is reported by Gibbon after the war.

V-002 "Reynolds Falls" (tick 28): Major General John F. Reynolds, commanding the left wing of the Army of the Potomac, was killed on the morning of July 1 as the Iron Brigade went into McPherson's (Herbst) Woods. Doubleday gives the hour as about 10:15 a.m., Howard's reports give 11:15, and the source of the shot is unsettled.

V-022 "Mudge and the Charge at Culp's Hill" (tick 483): On the morning of July 3 Colonel Colgrove sent the 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana across the open meadow in front of the Confederate breastworks on Culp's Hill. The 2nd Massachusetts lost about 130 killed and wounded, including its commander, Lieutenant Colonel Mudge, and the 27th Indiana 112. The hour is disputed and Mudge's reported last words come from survivors' later accounts.

V-020 "Custer at East Cavalry Field" (tick 539): East of Gettysburg on the afternoon of July 3 Stuart's cavalry met Gregg's division and Custer's Michigan Brigade while the infantry assault was made at the center. Lee's report says the cavalry 'effectually protected our left' and that Hampton was seriously wounded. The hour of the main charges (about 3 p.m. by one account) and Custer's reported shout are from later accounts.

V-019 "Pickett's Return" (tick 557): After the repulse Pickett's division came back across the fields. The Confederate return counts 2,888 casualties in it, 1,499 of them captured or missing (OR 27/2 p.339); Lee reports that Armistead and Garnett were killed and Kemper dangerously wounded. Pickett's remark that he had no division is a tradition from later accounts.

V-021 "Farnsworth's Charge" (tick 568): About 5 p.m. on July 3 Kilpatrick ordered Farnsworth's brigade to charge on the Confederate right south of the Round Tops, and Farnsworth was killed leading it. Farnsworth had been a brigadier general since June 29. Reports that he protested, and the words said to have passed between him and Kilpatrick, come from survivors' later accounts.

V-001 "The First Shot" (tick 12): About 7:30 a.m. on July 1, 1863, Lieutenant Marcellus Jones of the 8th Illinois Cavalry is traditionally credited with the first shot of the battle, fired from a borrowed carbine at a Confederate officer on the Chambersburg Pike. Other men claimed earlier shots, so the claim is contested; the Official Records credit Lieutenant Roder's gun of Calef's battery with the first artillery shot.

V-004 "The Railroad Cut" (tick 36): Lieutenant Colonel Rufus Dawes's 6th Wisconsin, with the 95th New York and the 14th Brooklyn, charged Davis's Confederates in the unfinished Railroad Cut north of the Chambersburg Pike. The men in the cut threw down their arms; the 6th Wisconsin sent to the rear 7 officers and about 225 men and took the 2nd Mississippi's flag.

V-014 "The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill" (tick 326): At dusk on July 2 Hays's Louisiana brigade and Hoke's North Carolina brigade, under Colonel Avery, charged Cemetery Hill from the town. Lee's report says they drove two lines from the fences, forced their way into the works on the crest and seized several pieces of artillery, but a heavy force advanced against their unsupported right and they were compelled to retire, bringing out about 100 prisoners and four stand of colors.
Lee's Headquarters: Near the Chambersburg Pike on Seminary Ridge.
Evergreen Cemetery gatehouse: Union headquarters area. Howard established headquarters here July 1. Evergreen Cemetery on the hill. (elevation 625 ft)
Triangular Field: Rocky field below Devil's Den. Ward's brigade fought here. Texas Brigade assault through this terrain. (elevation 560 ft)
Railroad Cut (unfinished railroad grade): Davis's brigade was in the cut when the 6th Wisconsin, 95th New York and 14th Brooklyn charged it on July 1; the Confederates in it surrendered.
Lutheran Theological Seminary: Cupola used for observation. Perrin's charge broke through Seminary grounds July 1.
Bliss Farm: Contested skirmish position between Seminary and Cemetery ridges July 2-3. Changed hands several times. Burned on July 3. (elevation 540 ft)
Bryan Farm: Adjacent to The Angle. Stood amid the fighting during Pickett's Charge.

Little Round Top: Key terrain on Union left. Vincent's brigade arrived just in time July 2. 20th Maine held the extreme left. The 140th New York under Col. O'Rorke came up and charged down the slope; O'Rorke was killed. Hazlett's battery was brought onto the summit. (elevation 650 ft)

Tour stop 12 "The Angle" (The High-Water Mark — July 3, about 3:30 PM; tick 549): About 3:30 PM on July 3 the survivors of the mile-long advance reached the stone wall at The Angle. By tradition Armistead raised his hat on his sword and called, "Come on, boys, give them the cold steel!" — words from survivors' later accounts. Led by Armistead, a part of his brigade crossed the wall and reached the guns of Cushing's battery. Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing, wounded in both thighs, had fought on for an hour and a half and was killed at the fence by his guns, Webb reports. Armistead fell wounded at the guns and was left within the Union lines, Harrow reports. A later account says that, told his old friend Hancock was wounded, he asked that his watch and effects be given to Hancock

Tour stop 15 "The High Water Mark" (The Copse of Trees — July 3; tick 555): A small copse of trees on Cemetery Ridge served as the visual aiming point for Pickett's Charge and has since become known as the High Water Mark of the Confederacy — the point of maximum Confederate penetration into the Union line. Monuments and markers at the copse of trees commemorate the assault. The Gettysburg Battlefield Memorial Association, chartered in 1864, preserved parts of the field; the federal government took over the ground when the park was established in the 1890s. General Lewis Armistead, who died after being wounded at the guns, is remembered by a marker near the copse of trees. Tour stop 14 "Pickett's Charge" (The Mile-Wide Advance — July 3, 3:00 PM; tick 538): About 1 PM on July 3, 1863 (1:07 by one count), at a given signal, Confederate artillery opened a heavy cannonade on Cemetery Ridge: nearly 150 guns in position by Pendleton's count, 100 to 125 or more by Union estimates. It lasted about two hours. At about 3:00 PM (accounts run from 2:00 to 3:00) the Confederate column, estimated by Hancock at more than 15,000 men, stepped from the tree line on Seminary Ridge and began the mile-wide advance. Pickett's division, Pettigrew's division, and Trimble's two brigades crossed the open ground under devastating artillery and musket fire. Tour stop 10 "Culp's Hill" (The Overnight Fight — July 2-3; tick 380): While the fighting raged on the Union left on July 2, Johnson's Confederate division attacked the right flank at Culp's Hill. Greene's New York brigade — 1,424 men by Geary's count, reinforced during the evening by detachments of the I and XI Corps — held the entrenched hill against Johnson's division. Greene's men benefited from the solid earthworks they had constructed, firing from protected positions while Confederate attackers struggled uphill through dense woods in darkness. The fight continued sporadically through the night. The XII Corps, back from the left, fought at daylight on July 3 to retake the works the Confederates held. Tour stop 16 "Confederate Avenue" (The Retreat — July 4-5, 1863; tick 610): On the night of July 4-5, 1863, the Army of Northern Virginia began its retreat toward Virginia. A long wagon train of wounded men (Imboden's postwar account puts it at 17 miles) moved through driving rain toward the Potomac crossing at Williamsport. Meade chose not to pursue aggressively. President Lincoln was deeply disappointed that Lee's army escaped across the Potomac; in a letter to Meade that he did not send he wrote that Lee had been "within your easy grasp". Lee's army crossed the swollen Potomac on July 14, escaping to Virginia. The Gettysburg campaign was over.
